biography.value:
Bowser — The Dragon-King Who Keeps Getting Up

Bowser is the creature who has defined the Mushroom Kingdom through opposition for longer than most of its current inhabitants have been alive. He is the villain of every story, the kidnapper in every legend, the fire-breathing turtle-dragon-king whose name is used to frighten children and whose actual presence frightens things considerably larger than children. He has fought Mario more times than either of them can accurately count. He has been defeated, imprisoned, exiled, launched into the sun, thrown into lava, dropped from airships, and subjected to indignities that would have destroyed any creature whose defining characteristic was anything other than the absolute, pathological refusal to stay down.

Bowser always gets back up. That's the thing about Bowser that makes him terrifying not as a villain but as a FACT. He doesn't stay defeated. He doesn't learn the lesson that everyone thinks defeat is supposed to teach. He stands up, dusts off whatever substance he was thrown into, returns to his castle, rebuilds whatever army Mario scattered, and starts planning the next attempt. The cycle has repeated for decades. The cycle IS Bowser. Without the cycle, he is a very large koopa with anger management issues and an empty castle.

Understanding what Bowser was—at his peak, before the current crisis reduced him from conqueror to captive to reluctant ally to vampire dinner guest—requires understanding the scale of his ambition and the genuine capability that made that ambition something other than delusion.

Bowser consolidated power in Darkland during the chaos following Princess Peach's assassination in 955 BF. While the Mushroom Kingdom fragmented into civil war factions, Bowser built. He unified the Koopa Troop—a loose confederation of koopa, goomba, and allied species—into a genuine military force through a combination of personal dominance, strategic marriages with subordinate clan leaders, and the kind of charismatic brutality that inspires loyalty in creatures who respect strength above all other qualities. By the time the First Bowser Conflict began in approximately 1005 BF, Darkland was the most organized military power in the region, and Bowser was its undisputed ruler.

The kidnapping obsession is the detail that historical analyses either focus on exclusively or dismiss entirely, and both responses miss the point. Bowser kidnapped Princess Toadstool (and later, during the brief period when "Peach" was used for her successor) repeatedly, obsessively, with a persistence that transcended tactical logic and entered the territory of something that psychologists would have opinions about if anyone ever convinced Bowser to attend a session.

The kidnappings were not rational. Bowser could have conquered Mushroom Kingdom territory through conventional military force at several points during the civil war period when the kingdom's defenses were at their weakest. He chose not to. Instead, he kidnapped princesses, built elaborate castle obstacles, positioned his subordinates in fortresses across eight worlds of territory, and WAITED for Mario to come. The entire invasion infrastructure was designed not to prevent rescue but to make rescue as dramatic as possible.

Waluigi—who has analyzed Bowser with the dedication of someone who has lost to him at every competitive event they've ever entered—believes the kidnappings were not conquest but courtship. Not romantic courtship in the conventional sense, but the courtship of someone who didn't know how to express desire except through control. Bowser wanted Peach (or her successor) the way he wanted everything: absolutely, unilaterally, without the complication of the other person's feelings or the recognition that relationships require consent rather than capture.

This interpretation doesn't excuse the kidnappings. It contextualizes them as the behavior of someone whose emotional development was shaped by a species and culture where taking what you want is the primary social mechanism, where strength determines entitlement, and where the concept of "asking" is foreign enough to require translation. Bowser didn't kidnap princesses because he was evil. He kidnapped princesses because his entire frame of reference for acquiring things he valued was "take them and defend your claim."

The Chaos Heart Crisis of 1025 BF represents the most complicated chapter of Bowser's history. He was one of the forced participants in the wedding that triggered the Chaos Heart's awakening—married to Princess Peach (the successor) against both their wills by Count Bleck. The ceremony was not about their feelings; it was about the conceptual union of opposing forces creating the paradox that empowered the Chaos Heart. Bowser was a tool. The experience of being USED—of having his agency removed and his body deployed as a component in someone else's plan—was transformative in ways that Bowser has never discussed and that observers have never adequately analyzed.

After the Crisis, Bowser's behavior changed in subtle but detectable ways. His invasion attempts became less frequent. His castle defenses became less elaborate. His interaction with Junior—always complicated by absence—acquired a quality that might have been guilt or might have been the recognition that empire-building costs things that can't be rebuilt. He still fought Mario. He still kidnapped (less often). He still roared and breathed fire and broke things. But something underneath the performance had shifted, the way a foundation shifts under a building that still looks solid from outside.

The current crisis has stripped away whatever remained of Bowser's pretensions to empire. He was captured aboard the Vigilance. He was traded between factions like cargo. He was taken captive by Wally (Waluigi's agent) and Bowser still doesn't fully understand the political dimensions of what happened to him. He attended Orangus Cornelius's vampire dinner party in the Shadowfell as a GUEST—not a conqueror, not an invader, a guest who followed etiquette because the alternative was worse. He examined necromancer wands with the curiosity of someone who has stopped pretending that magic beneath his station doesn't interest him.

He fought alongside the party at Raventree Manor. He participated in the Oracle's failed ritual. He has been scattered across dimensions by the Planar Fracture, reformed alliances with people he would have conquered a decade ago, and demonstrated capabilities and qualities that the Bowser of 1005 BF would have considered beneath his dignity. He has punched ghosts with his bare fists because Archie needed time to cast ice spells. He has accepted tactical direction from toads who weigh less than his left arm. He has cooperated.

This is the Bowser who exists now: still enormous, still fire-breathing, still capable of violence that makes architecture regret being built, but tempered by decades of defeat, by the loss of his empire, by the absence from his son, and by the creeping realization that the cycle of kidnapping and rescue and defeat was never going to give him what he actually wanted. What he actually wanted was connection. What he actually wanted was for someone to choose to be near him rather than being forced to be near him. What he actually wanted was something that his entire species and culture had no vocabulary for, and that his own behavior made impossible.

Bowser at his peak was a natural disaster with a crown. Bowser now is something more complicated and more dangerous: a natural disaster that's learning to think.
biography.public: A massive koopa dragon-king whose shell is scarred from decades of defeats he survived through stubbornness alone. He fills every room he enters, breathes fire when he's annoyed, and has recently started cooperating with people he used to try to conquer. This last development worries everyone, including Bowser.

description.value:
Bowser's primary weapons are attached to his body and have been since birth. His claws can rend steel, his fists can shatter stone, and his grip can crush things that were designed to be crush-resistant. He doesn't carry weapons because he IS a weapon—every component of his body optimized through species and personal development for the specific purpose of destroying whatever he's directed toward.

His fighting style is self-taught through decades of combat against the most capable hero the Mushroom Kingdom has ever produced. Mario forced Bowser to improve. Every defeat revealed a weakness that Bowser addressed for the next encounter. Every near-victory showed a strength that Bowser refined. The result is a combat capability that has been honed against the best possible opponent for over thirty-five years—not elegant, not subtle, but devastatingly effective against anything that hasn't been specifically trained to counter Bowser's particular combination of speed, power, and the unsettling creativity of someone who has learned to fight by losing to a genius.

The punching-ghosts incident at Raventree Manor demonstrated something that shouldn't be possible: Bowser physically striking incorporeal entities through sheer force of personality and the particular density of a fist that has been clenched in fury so many times that even spiritual beings recognize it as a threat. Whether this reflects magical contamination from decades of exposure to supernatural events or simply Bowser's refusal to accept that something can't be punched, the effect is the same: his attacks count as magical for purposes of overcoming resistance.
description.chat: Claws that have shredded castle walls and fists that have punched ghosts into acknowledging physical reality. He doesn't need weapons. He is one.

unidentified.name: Natural Weapons
unidentified.description: This creature's natural claws and fists deliver devastating force that somehow affects even incorporeal entities.

description.value:
Bowser's shell is not armor he wears but anatomy he was born with, reinforced through decades of combat that have deposited layers of impact-hardened keratin over the original structure. The shell's spikes are genuine defensive weapons—creatures that grapple Bowser from behind or attempt to mount his shell take 2d6 piercing damage at the start of each of their turns as the spikes dig into whatever flesh is pressing against them.

The shell provides AC 21 (natural armor) and is the primary reason Bowser has survived injuries that would have killed conventional creatures multiple times over. It has absorbed dragon fire, magical explosions, being thrown into stars (this happened at least twice, according to accounts Waluigi considers credible), and the specific kind of architectural collapse that occurs when a structure not designed to contain a Bowser fight is forced to contain one anyway.

The shell also serves as a vehicle. Bowser can withdraw into it and spin, converting himself into a projectile that deals devastating damage to anything in his path. This technique was developed during his fights with Mario and refined through the kind of iterative engineering that occurs when your enemy keeps finding new ways to dodge your fire and you need alternatives.
description.chat: The shell is scarred from every battle he's survived, each mark a defeat that would have killed something less stubborn. The spikes are a reminder that attacking him from behind is also a bad idea.

unidentified.name: Spiked Natural Shell
unidentified.description: A massive spiked shell that provides extraordinary natural armor and serves as both defense and weapon.

description.value:
Bowser withdraws into his shell and launches himself as a spinning projectile, crossing up to 40 feet in a straight line and devastating everything in his path. The technique combines the rotational force of his massive body with the spiked shell's cutting capability, creating a mobile hazard that shreds through obstacles and enemies with equal disregard.

Each creature in Bowser's path must make a DC 21 Dexterity saving throw. On a failure, a creature takes 4d10 + 8 bludgeoning damage plus 2d6 piercing damage from the spikes and is knocked prone. On a success, a creature takes half damage and isn't knocked prone but is pushed 10 feet to either side of Bowser's path. Objects and structures in the path take double damage as the spinning shell grinds through them.

After the spin, Bowser emerges from his shell in the space at the end of his path. He cannot use Shell Spin again until the start of his next turn, as reorienting from the spin requires a moment of recovery. This recovery period—approximately two seconds—is the window Mario learned to exploit during their fights, and it remains Bowser's most consistent vulnerability during combat.
description.chat: The shell spins, spikes blur into a circle of destruction, and everything between Bowser and his destination learns that standing in a dragon-king's path is a structural engineering problem, not a combat one.

unidentified.name: Spinning Shell Charge
unidentified.description: This creature can withdraw into its spiked shell and launch itself as a devastating projectile.

description.value:
Bowser leaps and slams his full weight into the ground, creating shockwaves that radiate outward in a 20-foot radius. The technique exploits the simple physics of dropping something extremely heavy from height—Bowser weighs enough that his landing registers on seismographic equipment from considerable distance. The shockwaves crack stone, shatter glass, and knock anyone who isn't braced off their feet.

Each creature within 20 feet of the impact point must make a DC 21 Strength saving throw. On a failure, a creature takes 3d10 + 8 bludgeoning damage and is knocked prone. On a success, a creature takes half damage and isn't knocked prone. The ground in the affected area becomes difficult terrain as cracks, rubble, and displaced material make footing treacherous.
description.chat: He goes up. He comes down. Everything between 'up' and 'down' ceases to be solid.

unidentified.name: Seismic Slam
unidentified.description: This creature can leap and slam the ground, creating shockwaves that damage and topple everything in a wide radius.

description.value: Bowser's jaws can close with force sufficient to sever limbs and crush armor. His bite attack is typically reserved for enemies who have gotten close enough to grapple or for situations where his claws are occupied. The bite is enhanced by the same biological furnace that produces his fire breath—targets bitten feel residual heat from the furnace's proximity, and the wound often cauterizes partially on infliction.
description.chat: Jaws close with the finality of a drawbridge slamming shut, heat radiating from a mouth that doubles as a furnace.

unidentified.name: Crushing Bite
unidentified.description: A devastating bite attack from jaws that radiate heat.

description.value:
Bowser has been defeated more times than any creature in documented history and has survived every single time. Thrown into lava, launched into stars, crushed by collapsing castles, dropped from airships at terminal velocity—he has experienced fatal events that would create multiple sequential deaths for conventional creatures and has emerged from each one angry, slightly singed, and ready for the next round.

Three times per long rest, when Bowser is reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 hit point instead. Each use of this ability produces a visible effect: his eyes burn brighter, his shell's spikes lengthen slightly, and the ground under his feet cracks from the physical manifestation of his refusal to accept defeat. He doesn't recover through healing or resilience. He recovers through STUBBORNNESS—the fundamental quality that defines him more than fire breath or strength or the crown he hasn't worn in months.

After using all three instances in a single combat, Bowser can be brought to 0 hit points normally. But by the time an enemy has put him down four times, the environment around the fight has typically been so thoroughly destroyed that continuing the engagement becomes an architectural concern rather than a tactical one.
description.chat: He falls. He gets up. He falls again. He gets up again. At some point the enemy has to decide whether killing Bowser is physically possible or just theoretically interesting.

description.value:
Bowser learns from every fight. This is the quality that makes him genuinely dangerous rather than merely powerful—a creature that simply hits hard can be countered, but a creature that adapts its approach based on what it learns from being countered is a problem that gets harder with each engagement.

After the first round of combat, Bowser gains advantage on attack rolls against any creature that has successfully hit him, as he's catalogued their attack patterns and adjusted his defense and positioning accordingly. After the second round, he gains resistance to the most common damage type he's received, as his body and tactics adapt to prioritize defense against demonstrated threats. After the third round, he can use a reaction to impose disadvantage on one attack roll against him per round, as his understanding of the enemy's patterns becomes comprehensive enough to predict and counter specific attacks.

This adaptation resets between combats as different opponents require different assessments. But the ABILITY to adapt doesn't reset—thirty-five years of fighting the most capable hero in the kingdom have built neural pathways for combat learning that other creatures simply don't possess.
description.chat: Hit him once and he learns your timing. Hit him twice and he learns your patterns. Hit him three times and he knows exactly what you're going to do before you do it.

description.value: Three times per day, when Bowser fails a saving throw, he can choose to succeed instead. He has been hit with everything—petrification, banishment, mind control, temporal displacement, the Chaos Heart's reality-warping effects—and he has shrugged off all of it through the same mechanism that keeps him alive: the fundamental, bone-deep refusal to be stopped by anything he hasn't decided to stop for.
description.chat: The effect hits. Bowser doesn't care. He has survived worse. He has survived EVERYTHING.

description.value:
Bowser can take 3 legendary actions, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary action can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn.

Claw Swipe (1 action): Bowser makes one claw attack against a creature within reach.

Roar (1 action): Bowser roars with force that shakes the room. Each creature within 30 feet that can hear him must succeed on a DC 18 Wisdom saving throw or be frightened until the end of its next turn. Creatures that have fought Bowser before have disadvantage on this save, having learned that the roar usually precedes something worse.

Fire Snap (2 actions): Bowser breathes a quick burst of fire at a single target within 30 feet. The target must make a DC 20 Dexterity saving throw, taking 6d6 fire damage on a failure or half on a success.

Unstoppable Advance (2 actions): Bowser moves up to his speed. This movement doesn't provoke opportunity attacks, and any creature in his path must succeed on a DC 21 Strength saving throw or be pushed 10 feet ahead of him and knocked prone. Objects in his path take 4d10 bludgeoning damage.

Giga Bowser Rage (3 actions, 1/day): Bowser draws on reserves of fury that temporarily increase his size from Large to Huge for 1 round. His reach increases to 15 feet, his damage dice increase by one size category, and he gains 30 temporary hit points. After this round ends, he returns to Large size and cannot use legendary actions until the start of his next turn.
description.chat: Between other creatures' heartbeats, Bowser acts—clawing, roaring, burning, advancing, growing. The dragon-king doesn't wait for his turn because waiting was never part of his personality.

description.value:
Bowser is not the creature he was in 1005 BF. Decades of defeat, the Chaos Heart Crisis, the loss of his empire, separation from his son, and the current crisis's forced alliances have produced changes that the old Bowser would have considered weakness and that the current Bowser is slowly, reluctantly beginning to recognize as growth.

He cooperates with people he would have conquered. He follows tactical direction from creatures he could crush with one hand. He attended a vampire dinner party and used silverware instead of his claws. He punched ghosts to buy time for a wizard he doesn't like because the situation required teamwork rather than dominance. Each of these moments represents a compromise with the version of himself that spent decades trying to take everything by force and learning, repeatedly, that force alone doesn't work.

This change is not complete. Bowser still defaults to aggression when stressed. He still thinks in terms of conquest and control. He still believes, on some level, that being the strongest should entitle him to whatever he wants. But the defaults are being overridden more frequently by something that looks suspiciously like judgment, and the beliefs are being contradicted by experiences that keep proving them wrong.

The party interacts with a Bowser in transition—not the villain they might expect from legends, not the ally they might want, but something in between that is figuring out what it is in real time. He will fight alongside them if the situation demands it. He will argue with them about tactics, objectives, and whether punching something is the correct response to a problem (his position: always yes). He will occasionally do something selfless and then immediately deny that selflessness was involved. And he will, in moments of quiet honesty, wonder what kind of king he would have been if he'd learned these lessons before he lost everything.
description.chat: The dragon-king who kidnapped princesses is learning to cooperate with toads. It's not comfortable. It's not natural. But it might be the thing that finally makes him the king he always wanted to be.

description.value:
Bowser allegedly owes Wario 50,000 gold pieces for "storage fees" related to keeping some of Bowser's treasure safe during a battle. The actual situation: Wario stole half of Bowser's treasure and is now charging Bowser to return the other half. Bowser is aware that this arrangement is extortion. Bowser has not killed Wario over it because—and this surprises everyone who knows both parties—Bowser finds Wario's audacity entertaining in a way that genuine enemies never manage. There is a grudging respect between them that neither would call friendship and both would deny if asked.

The debt appears in Wario's ledger, in Bowser's grudging acknowledgment, and in the bizarre political reality that these two creatures—one a former dragon-king, one a con artist with a coin press—have a business relationship that has survived longer than most of the factions currently fighting over the Mushroom Kingdom's future.
description.chat: Fifty thousand gold. For storing treasure he stole. And Bowser hasn't killed him for it. This might be the most confusing relationship in the entire crisis.

unidentified.name: Outstanding Debt Document
unidentified.description: A debt record between this creature and a notorious con artist, representing an extortion arrangement that both parties have somehow maintained through mutual grudging respect.

description.value:
Bowser's fire breath is the most iconic destructive capability in the Mushroom Kingdom, a weapon that has destroyed castles, routed armies, and—according to Waluigi's research—once ignited an entire lake through means that physicists still debate. The fire originates from a biological furnace unique to koopa dragon-kings, fueled by a diet that includes metals, minerals, and whatever else Bowser feels like eating. The flame temperature exceeds what organic biology should produce, suggesting either magical enhancement, evolutionary anomaly, or simple refusal to conform to the laws of thermodynamics.

Bowser exhales fire in a 60-foot cone. Each creature in the cone must make a DC 20 Dexterity saving throw, taking 12d6 fire damage on a failure or half on a success. The fire ignites flammable objects in the area that aren't being worn or carried. The breath weapon recharges on a roll of 5-6 on a d6 at the start of Bowser's turn.

The fire breath's destructive potential has been a strategic factor in every conflict Bowser has participated in. Castles are built to resist it. Armies train formations to scatter when the breath begins charging. And Mario learned, very early in their rivalry, that the three seconds between the inhale and the exhale are the most important seconds in any fight against Bowser—if you're not out of the cone by then, you're not getting out.
description.chat: He inhales. The air around him superheats. And then fire erupts in a torrent that turns architectural ambition into archaeology.

description.value: Bowser makes three attacks: two claw strikes and one bite, or two claw strikes and one Ground Pound, or one Shell Spin (which replaces his entire action). He can substitute his Fire Breath for any two attacks if it's available.
description.chat: Claws, teeth, weight, fire—every part of him is a weapon and they all arrive in the same round.

description.value:
Bowser has a son who is currently building a vehicle in the deepest workshop of Koopa Castle to come find him. Bowser doesn't know this. He doesn't know that Junior is worried, that Kamek is consolidating power over the Koopa Troop remnants, or that his son's mythology about an invincible father is crumbling under the weight of reality. He knows only that Junior exists, that Junior needs him, and that he's currently in a dimension where reaching Junior is impossible.

The separation from Junior affects Bowser's behavior in ways he doesn't acknowledge and barely understands. He becomes more reckless in combat when he feels purposeless—as though proving his strength to absent witnesses might somehow communicate across dimensions. He becomes more protective of small creatures when Junior's absence weighs heavily, transferring parental instinct to whatever vulnerable beings are nearby. And he becomes more cooperative with the party when he recognizes that cooperation might be the path back to his son, because returning to Junior is the one objective that overrides his pride, his aggression, and his stubborn independence.

If the party uses Junior as leverage—threatening his safety or promising to facilitate reunion—Bowser's response depends on whether the approach feels genuine. Genuine concern for Junior produces cooperation that nothing else can achieve. Manipulation using Junior produces violence that nothing can survive.
description.chat: Somewhere, his son is building something to come find him. Bowser doesn't know this. But something in his chest that isn't fire aches when he's quiet long enough to feel it.

description.value: The boneless needn't spend extra movement to move a creature it is grappling.

biography.value:
Goomba — The Ones Who Die First

The Goomba is the most common, most expendable, and most tragically undervalued member of the Koopa Troop's military structure. They are small mushroom-like creatures with no arms, stubby legs, prominent eyebrows that convey a permanent expression of mild indignation, and a combat life expectancy measured in seconds against competent opponents. Mario has personally defeated more Goombas than any living being has defeated anything, and the Goomba species has responded to this statistical reality with the kind of resigned determination that characterizes organisms whose survival strategy is volume rather than individual resilience.

Goombas serve as the Troop's conscript infantry—the bodies that fill formations, the patrols that walk corridors, the first wave that absorbs enemy attention while more valuable units position themselves. Their combat contribution is primarily absorptive: they exist to be engaged, to occupy enemy actions, and to die in ways that provide tactical information to the units behind them. "The Goomba learned that the enemy attacks with jumping" is a genuine entry in Koopa Troop tactical manuals, and nobody in the Troop's command structure considers this entry problematic.

The Goombas themselves have complicated feelings about their role. Many serve willingly because the Troop provides community, structure, and the sense of purpose that civilian Goomba life—which consists primarily of walking back and forth on platforms for reasons nobody has ever explained—does not offer. Others serve because conscription offers no alternative. And some serve with the quiet defiance of creatures who know they're cannon fodder and have decided to be the best cannon fodder possible, approaching their inevitable defeats with a professionalism that their commanders don't appreciate and that historians will never record.
biography.public: A small mushroom creature walking a patrol route with an expression of permanent mild annoyance, as though it knows exactly how expendable it is and has opinions about this that nobody asks.

description.value:
The Goomba's only attack is running into enemies headfirst, using its disproportionately hard cranium as a bludgeoning weapon. The headbonk is not sophisticated. It is not elegant. It is a small creature running at you with its head down and hoping that the impact accomplishes something useful. Against unarmored, distracted, or very unlucky targets, it occasionally does.

The headbonk's primary tactical value is distraction rather than damage. A Goomba headbonking an enemy forces that enemy to spend an action dealing with the Goomba rather than engaging more valuable targets. If the enemy stomps the Goomba (which typically requires one attack and deals any amount of damage, since Goombas have 7 hit points and AC 8), the Goomba has accomplished its mission: one enemy action consumed, one moment of tactical advantage created for the unit behind it.

Goombas who survive headbonk attempts are surprised and mildly confused by the experience. Success is not what training prepares them for.
description.chat: It runs at you head-first with the total commitment of someone who has accepted that this is probably the end and has decided to make it count.

unidentified.name: Headbutt
unidentified.description: A small creature charging headfirst with more determination than tactical viability.

description.value:
Goombas are critically vulnerable to attacks from above. Any attack that strikes a Goomba from a higher elevation—jumping attacks, falling objects, dropped items, gravity—deals double damage. This vulnerability is biological: the Goomba's cranium is hard for headbonking purposes but the body beneath is soft and compresses easily under downward force. A single stomp from a creature of Medium size or larger is typically sufficient to defeat a Goomba regardless of the attacker's strength score.

This vulnerability is so well-known that it defines the Goomba's tactical identity. They operate on flat terrain whenever possible. They avoid positions beneath ledges, balconies, or elevated platforms. They cluster together so that stomping one requires landing among the others, creating at least marginal retaliatory opportunity. And they maintain a permanent upward awareness that gives them advantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks to notice threats from above, a survival instinct honed by millennia of being the thing that gets stepped on.
description.chat: Don't stomp on them. They know you want to stomp on them. They've arranged their entire tactical doctrine around the assumption that you will try to stomp on them. Stomp on them anyway because it works every time.

description.value:
Goombas are individually negligible threats. In groups, they become something approaching dangerous through sheer volume—not because individual capability increases but because the number of actions required to eliminate them creates opportunities for more capable allies to capitalize on. When three or more Goombas are within 5 feet of each other and attacking the same target, each Goomba gains advantage on its headbonk attack roll as the collective assault from multiple directions makes effective defense more difficult.

This ability has saved Goomba lives exactly never, but it has delayed enemy advances, consumed enemy resources, and created the momentary distractions that Koopa Troopa squads behind them need to set up effective defensive positions. The Goombas don't know this. They think they're fighting. What they're actually doing is buying time with their bodies, and the Troop's tactical doctrine has been built around this function for so long that nobody questions whether it's ethical.
description.chat: One Goomba is a speedbump. Three Goombas are a slightly taller speedbump. Ten Goombas are a genuine tactical consideration, which is the most a Goomba can aspire to.

description.value:
Goombas are immune to the frightened condition. Not because they're brave—bravery implies a choice between fear and action, and Goombas don't experience that choice. They simply walk forward. They have always walked forward. Walking forward into danger is what Goombas do, the way breathing is what lungs do, the way falling is what dropped objects do. It is not courage. It is nature. And nature doesn't require saving throws.

This immunity makes Goombas unexpectedly useful against enemies who rely on fear effects. Dragon frightful presence, undead horrifying visage, banshee wailing—none of it stops a Goomba. The Goomba continues walking forward with its expression of mild annoyance, headbonking whatever terrifying entity it encounters with the same determination it would apply to a locked door or an unfamiliar obstacle. The Goomba doesn't understand why the dragon is surprised. The Goomba doesn't understand most things. The Goomba walks forward.
description.chat: It's not brave. It's not fearless. It simply doesn't have the cognitive architecture for fear to interrupt its walking-forward subroutine. The dragon is confused. The Goomba is not.

biography.value:
Hammer Bro — The Elite Who Earned It

Hammer Bros are the Koopa Troop's elite infantry—koopas who distinguished themselves through combat performance and were promoted to a specialized role that combines armored durability with ranged firepower through the ancient koopa art of throwing hammers at things until those things stop being problems. They wear helmets that standard Troopas don't receive, carry an apparently infinite supply of hammers that they produce from somewhere nobody has ever adequately explained, and operate in paired teams that coordinate their throws to create overlapping fields of hammers that make approaching them an exercise in pain avoidance.

The hammers are the mystery. Hammer Bros throw hammers continuously during combat—not one or two, but DOZENS, an unending stream of spinning metal that arcs over intervening obstacles and descends on targets with trajectories that defy simple ballistics. Where the hammers come from is the subject of intense speculation among Mushroom Kingdom intelligence analysts. Some theories suggest hammerspace—a pocket dimension from which the hammers are summoned. Others suggest rapid materialization through innate magic that Hammer Bros themselves don't understand. The most prosaic theory involves hidden compartments in the shell, which would explain the hammers but not the apparent unlimited supply.

Hammer Bros are proud. They earned their helmets through performance, and they maintain their status through continued excellence. A Hammer Bro who misses consistently is demoted to standard Troopa duty, which is considered humiliating enough to motivate accuracy that borders on supernatural. They work in pairs because paired Hammer Bros are exponentially more dangerous than individual ones—while one throws, the other repositions, creating a rotating barrage that never stops and never comes from the same angle twice.
biography.public: A helmeted koopa with an expression of professional determination and a hammer in each hand, with more hammers visible somewhere behind him in quantities that shouldn't be possible.

description.value:
The Hammer Bro's signature attack: a rapid-fire barrage of thrown hammers that arc over obstacles and descend on targets with trajectories calculated through instinct rather than conscious math. Each hammer is a standard construction hammer—metal head, wooden handle, nothing magical about it individually—but the VOLUME and ACCURACY of the throws transforms mundane tools into a devastating ranged attack.

As an action, a Hammer Bro throws two hammers at targets it can see within 40 feet. Each hammer requires a separate attack roll (+5 to hit) and deals 1d8 + 3 bludgeoning damage on a hit. The hammers arc over half cover and three-quarters cover (though not total cover), reflecting the Hammer Bro's trained ability to throw in parabolic trajectories that bypass obstacles between thrower and target.

The unlimited supply remains unexplained. After combat, hammers thrown by Hammer Bros are found at impact sites as normal, non-magical hammers. They don't disappear. They don't return. New ones simply appear in the Hammer Bro's hands when needed. Investigation into this phenomenon has been classified as "not worth the headache" by the Mages' Guild.
description.chat: Hammers arc through the air in quantities that shouldn't be possible, descending on targets with the inevitability of rain and considerably more impact.

unidentified.name: Infinite Hammer Throws
unidentified.description: This creature throws hammers in rapid succession from an apparently unlimited supply, arcing them over obstacles to reach targets.

description.value:
A reinforced helmet that distinguishes Hammer Bros from standard Troopas and provides protection against the overhead attacks that are the primary threat to koopa infantry. The helmet is earned through performance and maintained through continued excellence—losing or damaging a helmet without adequate justification results in demotion that carries social stigma among koopa military culture.

The helmet provides +1 AC (already calculated in the Hammer Bro's statistics) and grants immunity to the critical hit bonus damage from attacks originating above—the specific vulnerability that defines standard koopa infantry is partially mitigated for the elite who earned the right to wear head protection.
description.chat: The helmet says 'I earned this.' The dent in the helmet says 'and this is why I needed it.'

unidentified.name: Elite Infantry Helmet
unidentified.description: A reinforced helmet that marks its wearer as elite infantry, providing protection that standard soldiers don't receive.

description.value:
Hammer Bros operate in paired teams that coordinate their attacks for maximum effectiveness. When two Hammer Bros are within 15 feet of each other and attacking the same target, both gain advantage on their hammer throw attack rolls as the dual barrage from different angles makes effective dodging nearly impossible. Additionally, when one Hammer Bro of a pair is attacked, the other can use its reaction to throw a hammer at the attacker (+5 to hit, 1d8 + 3 bludgeoning damage), discouraging enemies from engaging either member of the pair individually.

Breaking a Hammer Bro pair—killing one, separating them, or forcing one to retreat—immediately reduces the survivor's effectiveness and morale. A lone Hammer Bro has disadvantage on attack rolls for 1 round after its partner is eliminated, as the coordination reflexes trained into paired operation produce hesitation when the expected partner isn't there.
description.chat: They work in pairs because paired hammers create patterns that single hammers can't. Breaking the pair is priority one. Surviving the pair is priority zero.

description.value:
Hammer Bros hop. It's part of their fighting style—a rhythmic bouncing that keeps them in motion, makes them harder to hit, and provides the elevated launch angle that allows their hammer arcs to clear obstacles. The hopping looks ridiculous from a distance and is extremely effective from combat range, as the constant vertical movement complicates targeting for enemies trying to return fire.

While hopping (which Hammer Bros do automatically during combat), attacks against them have disadvantage if the attacker is at the same elevation or lower. Attacks from above are unaffected—the hopping provides lateral evasion, not overhead protection. The hopping also allows Hammer Bros to move across gaps up to 10 feet wide without requiring ability checks, their rhythmic bouncing carrying them across spaces that would require standard Troopas to find alternate routes.
description.chat: Hop. Throw. Hop. Throw. The rhythm is annoying and effective in exactly equal measure.

biography.value:
Koopa Troopa — The Backbone Nobody Thanks

The Koopa Troopa is the standard infantry soldier of the Koopa Troop, the bipedal turtle-people who have served as Bowser's primary ground forces for as long as anyone can remember. They walk patrol routes. They man fortress positions. They stand between Mario and whatever objective Mario is stomping toward. And they die—in enormous numbers, with depressing regularity, respawning through mechanisms that nobody fully understands and that the koopas themselves describe only as "it's a turtle thing."

The average Koopa Troopa is not stupid, despite what the legends suggest. The average Koopa Troopa is a conscript or career soldier who signed on with the Troop because Darkland's economy offers limited alternatives and because Bowser's military provides food, shelter, and a shell-maintenance stipend that civilian life cannot match. They follow orders because the chain of command works, because the alternative is court martial, and because most of them genuinely believe in the Koopa Troop's mission even if they can't quite articulate what that mission is now that Bowser has been absent for weeks and Kamek is issuing orders that don't match what Bowser would have wanted.

Kamek's return to the Valley of Bowser on Highsun 18 has created a command crisis that the rank-and-file Koopa Troopas are navigating with the specific anxiety of soldiers who know something is wrong but don't have enough information to know what. Kamek is giving orders. The orders are legal under Troop command structure. But the orders don't feel right—they're focused on consolidation and control rather than rescue, on securing Kamek's position rather than finding Bowser, on preparing for something that Kamek hasn't explained. The Troopas follow because following is what they do. Some of them are starting to wonder whether what they do and what they should do have diverged.
biography.public: A bipedal turtle in standard Koopa Troop equipment, walking a patrol route with the resigned competence of someone who has been doing this job long enough to know it's thankless but not long enough to quit.

description.value:
Every koopa is born with a shell, and every koopa's shell tells the story of their life. Standard Troopa shells are green, smooth, and maintained according to Troop regulations that specify acceptable polish levels, damage repair protocols, and the specific angle at which rank insignia should be painted. A well-maintained shell is a source of pride. A damaged shell is a source of shame. A lost shell is a tragedy that most koopas would rather not discuss.

The shell provides AC 15 (natural armor) and allows the signature koopa defensive maneuver: withdrawal. As an action, a Koopa Troopa can withdraw fully into its shell, becoming a small, hard object with AC 18 and resistance to all damage except psychic. While withdrawn, the koopa cannot take actions, bonus actions, or reactions, and its speed is 0. Emerging from the shell requires a bonus action on a subsequent turn.

A withdrawn koopa can also be kicked, thrown, or otherwise used as a projectile by creatures strong enough to lift it. This is considered extremely rude in koopa culture and extremely effective in combat, dealing 2d6 bludgeoning damage to whatever the shell hits and 1d6 bludgeoning damage to the koopa inside.
description.chat: The shell is home, armor, and identity all in one. Taking care of it is the first thing a Troopa learns. Getting kicked while inside it is a risk they accepted when they signed up.

unidentified.name: Green Koopa Shell
unidentified.description: A natural shell that provides significant protection and allows full withdrawal for enhanced defense. The shell shows signs of regulation maintenance.

description.value: A standard-issue spear provided to Koopa Troop infantry, designed for koopa proportions and fighting styles. The spear is slightly shorter than human equivalent weapons, compensating for koopas' smaller stature while maintaining adequate reach to threaten enemies before they get close enough to stomp. The spearhead is mass-produced in Darkland foundries with quality that is adequate without being impressive—sharp enough for combat, durable enough for field conditions, replaceable enough that losing one doesn't require paperwork that takes longer than the battle did.
description.chat: Standard issue, standard quality, standard pointing-end-toward-enemy training. The spear does its job because the Troopa behind it does theirs.

unidentified.name: Military Spear
unidentified.description: A standard-issue spear of adequate quality, designed for small humanoid proportions.

description.value:
A Koopa Troopa can withdraw into its shell and launch itself at an enemy as a spinning projectile, sliding across the ground in a straight line up to 20 feet. One creature in the path must make a DC 12 Dexterity saving throw, taking 2d6 bludgeoning damage on a failure or half on a success. After the spin, the Troopa emerges from its shell in the space at the end of the movement, prone, and cannot take reactions until the start of its next turn.

The shell spin is the Troop's signature combat technique—every recruit learns it during basic training, practices it until the timing is automatic, and uses it in combat with the specific commitment of someone who knows that turning yourself into a projectile has inherent risks but also knows that the alternative is being stomped by something larger than you.
description.chat: The shell spins across the ground with the commitment of someone who has accepted that being a living cannonball is part of the job description.

description.value:
Koopa Troopas currently serve under Kamek's consolidated command following Bowser's extended absence. They follow orders because the chain of command requires it, but growing unease about Kamek's priorities—consolidation over rescue, control over search—has created a morale situation that could be exploited by parties who understand koopa loyalty structures.

Koopa Troopas who learn that Bowser is alive and that someone is actively trying to reach him become significantly more sympathetic to that someone's cause. A DC 13 Charisma (Persuasion) check can convince a Troopa to share information about Kamek's operations, patrol schedules, or defensive positions if the party demonstrates genuine intent to help Bowser. A DC 16 check can convince a Troopa to actively assist, though the assistance will be limited by the Troopa's fear of Kamek's magical capabilities.

Koopas who served directly under Bowser—veterans who remember his personal leadership rather than Kamek's proxy authority—are easier to turn (DC reduces by 3) because their loyalty is to the king rather than the institution.
description.chat: They follow Kamek because the rules say follow Kamek. They'd follow Bowser because their hearts say follow Bowser. The gap between rules and hearts is where opportunities live.

biography.value:
Magikoopa — The Troop's Magical Backbone

Magikoopas are the Koopa Troop's spellcasters—koopas who discovered magical aptitude and were trained in the traditions that Kamek established centuries ago. They wear blue robes, round spectacles that may or may not be prescription, and pointed hats that serve no magical function but have become traditional enough that going without one is considered professionally inappropriate. They ride broomsticks because Kamek rode a broomstick and tradition is tradition, though several younger Magikoopas have privately expressed interest in more modern transportation methods.

The Magikoopa magical tradition is distinct from the Mages' Guild's approach, from the Beanish magical systems, and from any other structured magical education in the region. Magikoopa magic is innate and species-specific—you either have the aptitude or you don't, and if you do, training refines it into a set of capabilities that includes shape-shifting objects, projectile energy blasts, and the teleportation that makes Magikoopas the Troop's most strategically mobile assets.

Standard Magikoopas serve as the Troop's magical support: healing wounded soldiers, enchanting equipment, providing magical reconnaissance, and—when combat requires it—delivering energy blasts that compensate for the Troop's otherwise limited ranged capability. They are not front-line combatants; their role is support and force multiplication, making other units more effective rather than winning engagements independently.

Kamek's return has energized the Magikoopa corps in ways that concern the Troop's non-magical personnel. The Magikoopas have always been loyal to Kamek before Bowser—he trained them, he established their traditions, he represents the magical heritage that gives their lives meaning. With Bowser absent and Kamek consolidating power, the Magikoopas' divided loyalty has become straightforward loyalty to Kamek, and their capabilities are being deployed according to Kamek's priorities rather than Bowser's standing orders.
biography.public: A robed koopa with round spectacles and a pointed hat, hovering on a broomstick with the dignified irritation of someone whose professional expertise is frequently undervalued by the non-magical soldiers they support.

description.value:
The Magikoopa's primary offensive spell: a shaped blast of magical energy that manifests as a geometric shape—typically a triangle, circle, or square—spinning toward the target with moderate speed and significant force. The shape is cosmetic rather than functional; all blast shapes deal the same damage. The variation exists because Kamek's original training manual included diagrams of different shapes and later generations of Magikoopas assumed each shape was a different spell rather than aesthetic options for the same effect.

The blast can be fired at a target within 60 feet as a ranged spell attack. On a hit, it deals 3d6 force damage. The damage type is force rather than elemental because Magikoopa magic operates on a fundamentally different principle than conventional arcane tradition—it manipulates reality directly rather than channeling elemental energies, which is why the blasts appear as abstract shapes rather than fire, ice, or lightning.
description.chat: A spinning geometric shape—today's shape is triangles—arcs toward the target with the professional precision of someone who has been doing this exact attack for their entire career.

unidentified.name: Geometric Energy Blast
unidentified.description: A ranged magical attack that manifests as spinning geometric shapes, dealing force damage through direct reality manipulation.

description.value:
Magikoopas can transform non-magical, non-attended objects into different objects of similar size and mass. A brick becomes a coin. A barrel becomes a Goomba (temporary, reverts in 1 hour). A rock becomes a mushroom that may or may not be edible depending on the Magikoopa's skill with the particular transformation. The spell requires an action and affects one object within 30 feet that the Magikoopa can see.

The transformations are temporary—lasting 1 hour before reverting—but they're useful for creating improvised resources, confusing enemies, and the specific kind of battlefield modification that turns a corridor full of barrels into a corridor full of hostile Goombas while the enemy is navigating it. The Goombas created this way are real enough to fight, die, and headbonk with genuine commitment to their brief existences, which raises philosophical questions that Magikoopas prefer not to address.
description.chat: The barrel becomes a Goomba. The Goomba walks forward with the resigned determination of its species. In one hour, it will become a barrel again. It does not know this. It does not need to know this.

description.value:
Magikoopas can channel healing energy into wounded allies, restoring hit points through the same reality-manipulation magic that powers their offensive blasts. As an action, a Magikoopa can touch a creature and restore 2d8 + 3 hit points. This healing can be used three times per long rest, after which the Magikoopa's magical reserves need time to regenerate.

Healing magic is the primary reason Magikoopas are valued by the Troop beyond their combat capabilities. Koopa field medicine is otherwise limited to bandages and rest, and having magical healing available during prolonged engagements significantly reduces casualty rates. Magikoopas are instructed to prioritize healing over offensive action when casualties mount, a protocol that some Magikoopas resent (they trained for combat, not nursing) and others embrace (keeping soldiers alive feels more meaningful than adding to the body count).
description.chat: The wounds close under magical attention, reality being convinced that the damage didn't happen through the same principles that throw geometric shapes at enemies.

description.value:
Every Magikoopa rides a broomstick because Kamek rides a broomstick and tradition is tradition. The broomstick provides a fly speed of 30 feet with hover capability, allowing Magikoopas to maintain elevated positions during combat and traverse terrain that ground-bound forces cannot cross. The broomstick is not magical in itself—the flight is powered by the Magikoopa's innate magic channeled through the broom as a focusing implement.

If the broomstick is destroyed (AC 10, 5 HP), the Magikoopa loses flight capability until it can obtain a replacement. Any broom of appropriate size works as a replacement—the magic is in the rider, not the implement—though Magikoopas are oddly particular about bristle quality and handle finish, treating their brooms with the same care that soldiers treat their weapons.
description.chat: The broom shouldn't fly. The koopa on the broom makes it fly anyway. Tradition and magic combine to produce hovering koopas with geometric opinions about combat.

unidentified.name: Flight Broom
unidentified.description: A broomstick used as a magical flight implement. The magic is in the rider, not the broom, but the rider is particular about broom quality anyway.

description.value: Briefly surrounded by silvery mist, you teleport up to 30 feet to an unoccupied space you can see.

reasons: Long-range weapon with no melee option → sniper

The lava-tunnel crew. The loyalists evacuated through the lava tunnel while the dragon held the outer approach; somebody has to make sure nothing follows them down it. A Bob-omb volunteers for that the way Bob-ombs volunteer for everything — once.

The sheet is a door that closes behind the survivors. It is also, if a player is feeling brave, the way to drop a corridor on a dragon's head.

The Bob-omb explodes and is destroyed. Each creature within 10 feet makes a DC 12 Dexterity saving throw, taking 4d6 fire damage on a failure or half as much on a success. Doors in the area stop being doors.

If the Bob-omb detonates in a corridor or tunnel 10 feet wide or narrower, the passage collapses behind it: impassable without ten minutes of digging, or a Wall Breaker. A creature in the collapsed squares makes a DC 12 Dexterity saving throw or takes 3d10 bludgeoning damage and is buried (restrained, prone).
If the Bob-omb takes fire damage or is reduced to 0 hit points by any other means, it detonates at the start of its next turn.

Ed agrees with Fred in principle and disagrees with him in every particular, which is how they have stayed alive this long. He is the one who remembers that nobody here built the switch, that old castles contain controls nobody remembers installing, and that there is an axe at the end of a river somewhere that this is going to come back to.

Steadier than he looks. Beside the king, or beside Sir Frankfurt, he holds; on his own he counts exits. Both are useful on a night like this.

One of the two Hammer Bros Bowser carried into a side room under his arms when the throne-room wall burst. The record gives the pair one question between them — does the castle have a self-destruct switch, and if the dragon is taking it anyway, could they not blow it up and walk the survivors to Neo Bowser City? — and does not say which of them asked it. This sheet gives Fred the proposal so the two can be played apart.

Bowser's answer was 'You want me to blow up my own castle?' Fred's position is that Mario once pressed a switch and a whole castle came down, so the technology exists. He is not wrong about the technology. He is a demolitions mind in a hammer-throwing body: his hammers find the weak course in a wall, and he can tell whether a switch does what its label says — which, tonight, matters.

From the record: the side room; the switch question; Mario once pressed a switch and a castle came down.

'Then the other boss arrived.' Nine Goombas and two Koopas were planning a retreat over an empty train track without their king when Koopa Killer Killa walked in and said that Killa was the boss. A Goomba objected that Killa was not Bowser. Nobody had appointed Killa. The empty space left by a retreating king was apparently enough to encourage the claim.

Not a traitor, not a loyalist — a vacancy with a club. He is the sideplot's complication: the remnant follows whoever spoke last, and he intends to be last. The name is as the record gives it; the archive has not asked which Koopas he has killed, or whether the title is aspirational.

From the record: Killa answered that Killa was the boss — Toad Town Station, the empty track.

Goombas and Koopas within 30 feet who can hear him and have no king in sight treat him as the boss: they have a +1 bonus to attack rolls while he is conscious and standing. The moment Bowser — or anyone they trust more — is visible, the bonus ends, and so, usually, does the arrangement.

Not a separate person. Omega Bowser is what happens when Bowser's Castle lands on Bowser. The present-day Bowser is a player character at level 8 in the XP ledger; this sheet is his second form for one night, built Gargantuan because the GM asked for a Bowser that is big when the walls come in.

The trigger. When Bowser (the PC) would be reduced to 0 hit points by bludgeoning damage from a collapsing floor or wall, from a falling tower, or from the crush of a Huge or larger creature — the dragon's Wall Breaker, the Switch Hag's countdown, Fawthful dropping the gallery — the GM may call the Omega instead of unconsciousness. The rubble heaves; the thing that stands up fills the room.

The swap. In Foundry, right-click Bowser's token → Transform and drop this sheet on him (keep mental scores), or swap the token for a 4×4 Omega token and run this sheet beside his. Omega starts at full hit points, in the space where Bowser was buried, with his own Legendary Resistances.

The clock. The form lasts 10 rounds, or until Omega Bowser drops to 0 hit points. Then Bowser comes back in the nearest free space: prone, with 1 hit point plus his Constitution modifier for each round the Omega lasted, and one level of exhaustion. Anything Omega was holding falls free. Nothing else carries back.

CR 14 is deliberate: for ten rounds he outclasses the dragon (CR 12) and Fawthful (CR 9) together, which is the point of being crushed by your own castle. He is not a tool for the rest of the campaign.

From the record: Bowser's fire breath and ground pound in the courtyard; the wall that finally burst; a king who kept going back to the breach.

A Hammer Bro who guarded a room because Bowser told him to, and was still guarding it when the order was retracted too late to matter. The dragon asked him where Bowser was; he answered in Draconic that he was not the target, and then he told it his family history until it stopped being able to think.

Sir Frankfurt the fourteenth — or the fiftieth, depending on which part of the count he reaches first — and the tenth child of twenty-four. His father charged Mario and died before the third world was over; his mother died of grief a few days later; Bowser took in the surviving children.
